newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: GOVT SAYS IT WON'T BE STEAM-ROLLED ON COLSTON
The Federal Government says it will have no hesitation in handing the Colston affair to the Federal Police if there are grounds for investigation, but the proper procedures must be satisfied first.
Administrative Services Minister David Jull says a call by the Federal Police Union to bring in police is merely political meddling.
Mr Jull says Senator Mal Colston has until April 18 to present his case.
The Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says the investigation process has gone on for long enough, reaching a point where only the police can take it further.
Mr Beazley says the police union's call follows comments by the Clerk of the Senate, Harry Evans, suggesting the matter's now beyond the investigative capacity of the senate.
BEVIS ASKS WHY AMERICAN SOLDIER WERE INVOLVED IN ARRESTS

Opposition Defence spokesman Arch Bevis has called for the Defence Minister to investigate why American military police were involved in the arrest of civilians in Ipswich, west of Brisbane, last month.
A security video from the Ipswich mall shows the U-S personnel assisting police in the arrest of a group of Aborigines.
Mr Bevis says the Status of Forces Agreement only allows US military police to assist local civilian police with American Defence personnel.
He says there seems to have been a serious breach of the agreement.
Mr Bevis says Defence Minister Ian MacLachlan should explain what's being done to prevent military police intervening in civilian matters.
PHAR LAP NOT TO BE MOVED OUT OF MUSEUM OF VICTORIA
The hide of Australia's most famous race horse, Phar Lap, will not be moved out of the Museum of Victoria, even though the building's to be closed for three years.
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says the Museum's most famous exhibit will stay where it is until the new Museum opens at the Carlton Gardens in the year 2000.
His announcement puts paid to suggestions Phar Lap should be moved to the Racing Museum of Victoria, the MCG, or even Crown Casino.
Mr Kennett has told Parliament the furtherest the race horse will move this year is to a lower floor.
BIGGEST GROUP OF NEW MIGRANTS FROM NZ - STUDY FINDS
A new study has found that just over 99-thousand new immigrants arrived in Australia in 1995/96, an increase of 13-per cent.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics study found that for the first time on record, the biggest group of new migrants to Australia has come from New Zealand, rather than the United Kingdom.
New Zealanders made up 12-per cent of Australia's immigration intake for the year, with more than 12-thousand people crossing the Tasman.

But more than a third of Australians, or 10-thousand people, permanently left the country, to settle in New Zealand. China accounts for Australia's largest growing immigration intake, with arrivals tripling between 1994 and 1996 to 11,200.
SETTLEMENT REACHED IN 4 CORNERS CASE
A settlement has been reached in the case where a Brisbane solicitor was suing the ABC and Four Corners journalist Chris Masters for defamation.
Tony Bailey took out the action following the screening of a report entitled "Lawyers, Drugs and Money", in March 1993.
The program alleged Mr Bailey had used more than a million dollars of the proceeds of drug money to fund the defence of two American drug traffickers, arrested in Brisbane for importing cannabis.
An ABC spokesman says the settlement was favourable to the ABC, while Mr Bailey's solicitor also said his client was happy with the terms.
BEAZLEY SAYS OTHER APEC COUNTRIES MUST MATCH TARIFF CUTS
Federal Opposition leader Kim Beazley says Labor wants to see other countries match Australia's lead in dropping tariff reductions, and give Australians a break.
The Opposition has indicated strongly it'll oppose tariff reductions for the textile industry unless there's evidence other countries also are dropping their trade barriers.
Mr Beazley says for the past 10 years, Australia has unilaterally moved to cut protection levels, something he says which hasn't been matched by APEC countries.
The textile, clothing and footwear industries fear the Industry Commission will recommend tariffs be cut to five per cent by the year 2005.
Mr Beazley warns that'll cost jobs in regional Australia, unless the cuts are matched by other countries.
